lab_title: Structural Anatomy of the Human Heart and Blood Flow Pathways
top_level_objectives: Identify the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels of the heart and locate them in 3D space.
Trace the sequential path of deoxygenated and oxygenated blood through the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
Explain how valve structure prevents backflow and relate ventricular wall thickness to functional workload.

scenes.scene_name: 1. Orientation: situating the heart in the thorax
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the 3D heart model in anatomical orientation so students can reliably identify anterior/posterior, base/apex, and the heart's relation to the lungs and ribcage. Learning objective: orient the model and use AR controls to manipulate view.
key_visuals: Full-color 3D heart centered in a semi-transparent thoracic cavity (rib cage, lungs faded) — heart apex pointing down and left; base toward the superior thorax
Floating orientation gizmo (anterior/posterior/left/right) and scale indicator (actual size vs magnified)
Text labels for 'Apex', 'Base', 'Anterior surface' that fade on interaction
student_actions: Rotate, pan, and scale the heart to view from multiple angles; use the orientation gizmo to return to standard anatomical view
Tap the 'Apex' and 'Base' labels to hear short descriptions (play 'Label_Apex.mp3', 'Label_Base.mp3')
Place the model within the AR scene at a suggested distance (e.g., 0.5–1.0 m) using an on-screen placement guide

scenes.brief_purpose: Identify and distinguish the major vessels entering and leaving the heart (SVC, IVC, pulmonary arteries/veins, aorta, pulmonary trunk). Learning objective: recognize vessel positions and their roles in systemic vs pulmonary flow.
key_visuals: Heart with color-coded vessels: systemic veins in blue (SVC, IVC), pulmonary arteries in blue, pulmonary veins in red, aorta in red; labels anchored to vessel origins
Pulsing animation on vessels synced to heartbeat to show flow direction
Callout panels for each major vessel with brief text and audio: 'Vessel_SVC.mp3', 'Vessel_Aorta.mp3'
student_actions: Tap each major vessel to highlight and expand a callout showing name, direction of flow arrow, and one-line function
Toggle ‘show only systemic’ / ‘show only pulmonary’ overlays to see grouping
Use a ‘trace’ tool to draw a highlighted line from a selected vessel to its insertion point on the heart

scenes.brief_purpose: Expose internal chamber anatomy (right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle) and show relative sizes and chamber boundaries. Learning objective: identify the four chambers and distinguish atria from ventricles.
key_visuals: Cutaway/transparent myocardium revealing internal cavities with color-coded chambers (RA, RV, LA, LV) and floating text labels
Perspective that shows interatrial and interventricular septa and valve orifices
Short audio descriptions for each chamber: 'Chamber_RA.mp3', etc.
student_actions: Swipe to open a longitudinal cutaway that separates the heart into front/back halves for interior view
Tap each chamber to lock a label and hear a 10–15 second summary of its role
Select a chamber to display its approximate resting volume range and receive a prompt to rank chambers by wall thickness

scenes.scene_name: 4. Valves up close and one-way function
scenes.brief_purpose: Examine the four valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, aortic), their leaflets, and how they prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle. Learning objective: identify each valve and describe its role in directional blood flow.
key_visuals: Close-up animated views of each valve in cross-section showing cusps/leaflets and chordae tendineae where present
Synchronized valve animation during a simulated heartbeat showing opening and closing, with arrows indicating flow
student_actions: Play/pause the cardiac cycle and step to diastole or systole to observe valve positions
Manually open/close individual valves to see how backflow is prevented and view a slowed animation of leaflet coaptation
Answer an interactive prompt: 'Which valve prevents backflow into the left atrium during ventricular contraction?' and receive feedback

scenes.scene_name: 5. Tracing blood flow — the dual-loop circulation
scenes.brief_purpose: Guide students through the sequential path of deoxygenated and oxygenated blood through the heart, lungs, and systemic circulation using animated tracers. Learning objective: accurately trace the path and name each chamber, valve, and vessel encountered in order.
key_visuals: Animated colored particles: blue particles for deoxygenated blood, red for oxygenated, moving along the exact pathways
Stepwise callouts that light up as the tracer reaches: RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → LA → mitral → LV → aortic valve → aorta
A small inset timeline showing current step number and expected next step
student_actions: Start the 'Trace' mode which automatically sends a particle and pauses at each anatomical landmark; at each pause, choose the correct next valve/vessel from 3 options to continue
Manually drag a tracer bead through the heart following prompts to reinforce sequence
Toggle labels on/off to move from guided to unguided tracing for assessment

scenes.scene_name: 6. Functional implications: ventricular thickness and clinical context
scenes.brief_purpose: Compare left and right ventricular wall thickness, relate structure to function and pressure demands, and explore consequences of valve failure or increased afterload. Learning objective: explain why the left ventricle is thicker and predict effects of valve dysfunction or increased systemic resistance.
key_visuals: Side-by-side cutaway comparison of RV and LV showing measured wall thickness overlays (mm) and a pressure gauge indicating typical systolic pressures
Simulated contraction strength and myocardial strain animation demonstrating higher force in LV
Clinical vignette pop-up illustrating regurgitation when a valve fails with animated backflow
student_actions: Toggle measurement overlays to view and compare numerical wall thickness and typical pressures for each ventricle
Run a short simulation increasing afterload to observe required increase in LV work and see the effect on stroke volume
Complete a 3-question reflection: identify the structural reason for LV thickness, predict outcome of mitral regurgitation, and summarize how valves maintain unidirectional flow
